title: Getting the Details Just Right: Highlighting
author: Watson, Andrew
source: Learning and the Brain Blog (learningandthebrain.com), September 3, 2023
summary: Andrew Watson revisits highlighting research, starting from Dunlosky and colleagues' decade-old conclusion that highlighting has "low utility" and can even hurt performance on tasks requiring inference, before turning to a more recent 2022 meta-analysis by Ponce, Mayer, and Mendez that adds crucial nuance. That meta-analysis isolates two variables the earlier summary missed: student age or grade, and who does the highlighting. Its key finding is that instructor-provided highlighting benefits both college and K-12 students, but student-generated highlighting only benefits college students, not K-12 students, because younger students typically don't yet know which ideas are actually important. Watson adds a second, more surprising finding from the same meta-analysis: reviewing previously highlighted text later does not improve learning significantly more than simply reading or studying the text again, meaning highlighting's value, if any, comes from the act of focused attention during first reading, not from the resulting markings as a later study aid. He shares his own practice as an English teacher, asking students to circle very specific, sparse textual patterns rather than open-ended highlighting, as an example of the meta-analysis's recommendation that highlighting needs explicit training and tight constraints to be useful, especially with younger students.
points: Watson's central update to received wisdom is that highlighting isn't uniformly low-value; it depends heavily on who does it, with instructor highlighting helping K-12 students where student highlighting does not.

His second key finding, that reviewing old highlights doesn't outperform simply re-reading, undercuts the common assumption that the payoff from highlighting comes later, at review time, rather than during first reading.

His own classroom example, circling three or four specific recurring words or symbols in a text, operationalizes the meta-analysis's call for narrow, trained highlighting rather than open-ended "highlight what seems important."
He explicitly ties the finding back to a companion piece on retrieval practice, arguing "review the highlights" should be replaced by retrieval practice as a study strategy.
quotes: we rate highlighting and underlining as having low utility. In most situations that have been examined and with most participants, highlighting does little to boost performance.
If the INSTRUCTOR does the highlighting, doing so benefits college students AND K-12 students, but If the STUDENT does the highlighting, doing so benefits college studets but NOT K-12 students.

Students — especially younger students — probably don’t know what the important ideas are. For that reason, their own highlighting might not accentuate important ideas (on average), and so they don’t benefit from highlighting.
on average, reviewing highlighted text previously highlighted by learners did not improve learning significantly more than students who only read or studied the text.
Another conclusion is less of a surprise: training helps. That is: we can help students (yes, even K-12 students) highlight more effectively.
